beats.text: Main idea questions aren't asking what the passage mentions. They're asking what it's for.
Ask yourself: if I could keep only one sentence, which one explains why all the others are there?
The main idea is almost never handed to you up top. You build it from the whole passage.
Wrong answers usually grab one small detail, or go so vague they could describe a totally different passage.
Here's one. Read it with me.
Before this part, the team thought temperature was the big threat. Then fifteen years of data changed their minds.
Genetically diverse reefs survived the heat waves. Uniform ones didn't. And the last sentence turns that into advice: protect diversity, not just temperature.
Temperature as the biggest threat? That's the belief they moved past. And how long they studied is true, but it's just a detail.
A wide variety of threats could describe any reef article ever written. It never mentions what this study found.
Genetic diversity, not temperature alone. That's the finding and the point, so that's the answer.
Passages love to open with an idea just so they can overturn it. Don't pick the idea they overturned.
Find the sentence that makes all the others make sense. Then pick the choice that says it. No bigger, no smaller.
Detail questions don't want your opinion. They want you to find one sentence and say it back accurately.
However the question is worded, the move is the same. Find the sentence that answers it, then read it again.
The right choice says what that sentence says. No outside knowledge, no flipped direction, no bigger claim.
Slowing isn't stopping. Some isn't all. If a choice makes the finding sound stronger, be suspicious.
Here's one. Read it with me.
The question asks what she found, not what she did. The finding is right here: thirty-four of the forty came back.
Tagging turtles over two years is what she did. It's true, but it isn't a finding.
All forty? The text says thirty-four, so that's overstating it. And six is the number that didn't come back.
Thirty-four of forty, exactly the way the text says it. Nothing added, nothing flipped.
Six and thirty-four both describe this study. Only one answers the question. Go back and check instead of trusting memory.
Find the sentence, read it again, and pick the choice that says the same thing at the same strength.
Stories and poems feel harder, but the question is the same one: what does the text actually show?
Go by what the character actually does and says. Not by what a character like that would usually feel.
Nervous doesn't always mean unhappy. Silence doesn't always mean disapproval. Let the text tell you.
And don't add a motive or a habit the text never mentions, no matter how believable it sounds.
Here's one. Read it with me.
Setup: Wen's grandfather just paid for a stranger's groceries. Then he tells no one. Not even his wife.
When Wen brings it up, he gives a short answer and picks up the paper. He's closing the subject.
Wanting recognition is the opposite of telling no one. And regularly? We only see him do this once.
Disapproves of his grandson? He's dodging the topic, not scolding anyone. Nothing shows he's annoyed at Wen.
He keeps his kindness private. That matches everything he actually does.
A short reply feels cold, so disapproval sounds right. But the text only shows him keeping something private.
Stick to what the character does and says. If the text doesn't show it, don't pick it.
Conclusion questions ask for something the text never says out loud. But it has to follow from what it does say.
Take two facts the passage gives you and put them together. The conclusion lives where they meet.
It has to follow from the text, not just sound plausible. If the text could be true and the choice false, drop it.
Wrong answers add outside information, make the conclusion stronger than it is, or flip what caused what.
Here's one. Read it with me.
Fact one: ninety-one percent of people who tried the bike-share would use it again. They like it.
Fact two: only twelve percent of residents have tried it at all. So most people haven't given it a shot.
Most residents dislike it? We don't know what non-users think. Not trying something isn't the same as disliking it.
Getting canceled, being too expensive: the text never mentions either one. Those choices are invented.
Liked by the people who tried it, but most haven't tried it yet. Both facts, nothing extra.
Low usage makes dislike sound reasonable. But reasonable isn't enough. The text has to back it up.
Put the stated facts together and pick the choice that follows from them. Nothing added, nothing stretched.
Which choice best supports this claim? It's an easy question to ask, and a sneaky one to answer.
Before the choices, pin down what the claim is actually about. That's the thing your evidence has to measure.
Fast filter: cross out anything that's just a general statement about the topic. That's bait.
Of what's left, pick the specific number that measures the claim's exact outcome. Related isn't enough.
Here's one. Read it with me.
The claim: the bike lanes reduced traffic congestion. So we need a number about congestion.
Cyclists feeling safer is a feeling, not a traffic measurement. That one's out.
Twelve million dollars and forty miles are real numbers. But one measures spending, the other measures size. Neither is congestion.
Commute times fell fifteen percent. That's a number about congestion, tied to the bike lanes.
A big, specific number feels like strong evidence. It isn't, unless it measures what the claim is about.
Find what the claim says changed. Then pick the number that measures that change.
Some claims say one thing caused another. Those need tougher evidence than a nice number.
When a claim says caused or led to, the evidence has to rule out other explanations.
The best way is a comparison: a similar group that didn't get the change, and didn't see the result.
Something dropping after a change doesn't prove the change did it. Something else could have happened at the same time.
Here's one. Read it with me.
The claim: the training reduced injuries. That's a cause, so we need to rule out other causes.
A two-hour session and a helpful rating don't measure injuries at all. Those go first.
Injuries fell eighteen percent. Sounds good. But maybe production just slowed down that year. This choice can't rule that out.
Same eighteen percent drop, plus a sister factory without the training that saw no change. That rules out a company-wide slowdown.
A clean before-and-after number is tempting. For a cause claim, it only shows two things happened around the same time.
When the claim says caused, look for the choice with a comparison group. It's the one that rules things out.
Graph questions don't need tricks. They need you to read the numbers slowly.
Find the exact category or time period the question points to before you look at the choices.
Then check each choice against the data. Don't stop at the first one that sounds plausible.
Wrong answers swap a label, flip a direction, or stretch one small change into a whole trend.
Here's one. Read it with me.
We need what happened after quarter two. Revenue went from five point one down to four point eight. A small dip.
Then quarter four jumps to six point three. So it dipped, then rose again.
Rose in every quarter misses the dip. Remained flat ignores that anything changed at all.
Fell in every quarter takes one dip and stretches it through the whole year. Quarter four went up.
Fell slightly, then rose again. That's exactly what the numbers do.
One small drop can get stretched into a claim that it fell every quarter. Check each number before you believe a pattern.
Find the part the question asks about, read the actual numbers, and match them one by one.
Picking the best quote isn't about finding the most dramatic line. It's about finding the most exact one.
First, figure out exactly what the claim names. Not just a feeling, but the specific kind of feeling.
Then find the quote that actually shows that thing, not one that just mentions the same person or scene.
Here's one. Read it with me.
The claim isn't just pride. It's quiet pride. That word quiet is doing a lot of work.
Eleven hours on beadwork is a fact with no feeling in it. And wondering if anyone will notice? That's doubt.
Telling the whole shop it's her finest dress is pride, sure. But it's loud. The claim says quiet.
Holding it up, saying nothing, smoothing one seam. That's pride, and it's quiet.
The loudest quote grabs your attention first. Often the quieter one matches the claim better.
Pin down exactly what the claim describes, then pick the quote that shows that, not just something close.
Some evidence questions give you findings that don't exist yet. Your job is to judge which one would matter.
Ask yourself: if this claim is true, what would we expect to see? Say it in your own words first.
Then pick the finding that matches that prediction exactly. Being about the same topic doesn't count.
If the question says weaken, look for the opposite of your prediction, or the same result without the cause.
Here's one. Read it with me.
The claim: the new line means fewer people drive downtown for work. So we'd expect less downtown driving after it opened.
Three years to build, and riders liking the comfort. Neither one tells us anything about driving.
Forty thousand riders a day sounds huge. But they could be new commuters who never drove. It doesn't show driving dropped.
Downtown parking permits dropped after the line opened. Fewer permits means fewer people driving in. That's the prediction.
Ridership is about the train, so it feels relevant. But the claim is about driving. Match the prediction, not the topic.
Turn the claim into what you'd expect to see. Then pick the finding that shows exactly that.
Fill-in-the-blank inferences reward the careful answer, not the exciting one.
The answer has to follow from the text alone. No outside knowledge, no creative leaps.
Ask what must be true next, given only what's here. Not what would be interesting.
Here's one. Read it with me.
The key fact: these results contradicted decades of research. That's surprising, and surprising results need checking.
Abandoning the whole question overreacts. And publishing right away skips the checking.
One result can't show decades of research were done wrong. The text never makes that leap.
Replicating the experiment. It's the cautious next step, straight from the text.
Breakthroughs and big reversals sound exciting. The right answer is the one the text forces.
Stick to the text, and pick the smallest step it supports.
Some inference questions hand you two facts and quietly expect you to use both.
Keep each fact separate, then ask what they add up to together.
The answer is the narrowest conclusion all the facts support. Not a sweeping one.
Here's one. Read it with me.
Fact one: three times as many loaves per batch. Fact two: it heats up in half the time.
More bread per batch, less waiting per batch. So output dropping, or staying the same, goes against both facts.
And customers never come up. The question is how much bread the bakery can make.
Output could go up a lot, without necessarily hiring more staff. Both facts, nothing extra.
Stop after fact one, and extra choices start to look fine. The second fact is there for a reason.
Line up every fact, and claim no more than they show together.
These look like vocab questions. Mostly, they're about finding one clue.
Cover the choices. Look for the clue: a contrast, a restatement, or a cause and its result.
Guess your own plain word for the blank. Then pick the choice that means it, not the fanciest one.
Here's one. Read it with me.
The clue: departments wanted bigger budgets, and they criticized the approach. So spending was tight. My word: strict.
Generous is the opposite. Nobody hoping for more money complains about generosity.
Confusing and enthusiastic don't explain the complaint. It's about how little got spent.
Austere means strict and bare-bones. That matches my word.
A harder word isn't more likely to be right. Pick the one that means what the sentence needs.
Find the clue, predict your word, then match it.
Sometimes the right answer looks wrong, because you only know its everyday meaning.
The test likes words with two common meanings, and then it uses the less familiar one.
If a choice seems too easy, or makes no sense at first, check its other meaning.
Here's one. Read it with me.
The critic recommended the film, but spent three paragraphs on its flaws. So the review was mixed.
Glowing is too positive for all those flaws. Dismissive is too negative, since the critic still recommended it.
Brief doesn't fit three paragraphs of flaws. And qualified? You probably hear credentials. That's the wrong meaning here.
Qualified also means held back by reservations. Praise with conditions. That's this review.
Know only one meaning, and you'll cross off the right answer without a second thought.
When a choice seems off, try its other meaning. The sentence tells you which one it wants.
Here, every choice is a real meaning of the word. Only one fits this sentence.
Cover the choices, reread the sentence, and put your own simple word in its place.
Then swap each choice in. Unusual meaning or everyday one, let the sentence decide.
Here's one. Read it with me.
She has a keen eye for small faults. She spots a crooked hem from across the room. My word: sharp-sighted.
Keen can mean eager. But an eager eye wants something. It doesn't spot a crooked hem.
Sharp-edged is for a blade, and bitterly cold is for a keen wind. Neither describes an eye.
Perceptive. Good at noticing things, which is exactly what she does.
Every wrong choice is a real meaning of keen. It just breaks when you swap it in.
Say it in your own words, then keep the choice that says the same thing.
Main purpose questions don't ask what a text is about. They ask what it's doing.
Sum up the whole text as a verb phrase, like to explain a discovery, or to show how someone feels.
In a story, ask what the details add up to. Usually a feeling, a place, or a relationship.
Here's one. Read it with me.
It's Mira's first time at the coast. She stops and stares, and the water seems endless. The rest of the scene keeps building that wonder.
Scared? Nothing says so. She lets go of her uncle's hand to stand and stare. That's awe.
The text never says why the family came. And the pictures she'd seen get one line, just to show the real ocean beats them.
To convey Mira's amazement at seeing the ocean for the first time.
A choice that fits one detail isn't the purpose. It has to cover the whole text.
Name what the whole text is doing, then match the verb and the aim.
Some questions don't care what a sentence says. They care what job it's doing.
A sentence might introduce a claim, give an example, or qualify one, meaning limit it without rejecting it.
The best test: delete it in your head. What would the passage lose?
Here's one. Read it with me.
The claim: narrow streets slow drivers, so they're safer. Then our sentence, starting with however.
Delete it, and narrow streets sound safer no matter what. It adds a condition: no clear sightlines, more risk.
It never says narrow streets are always more dangerous. There's no statistic. And sightlines aren't a new topic.
It qualifies the main claim. It limits it without throwing it out.
A however sentence often just limits a claim. Don't read it as a full contradiction.
Don't restate the sentence. Ask what the passage would lose without it.
Same idea as a sentence's job, just bigger. What is this paragraph there to do?
A paragraph usually gives background, raises an opposing view, offers evidence, or draws a conclusion.
Look at the paragraphs around it. Words like however and for example are big clues.
Here's one. Read it with me.
Paragraph one starts with: many people assume. Paragraph two starts with: in reality. Belief, then correction.
No invention history here. And the passage never says rods don't work, just not like a decoy.
It's not a rare exception either. It's a belief lots of people share.
It presents a common misconception, and sets up the real explanation that follows.
Skim past a phrase like in reality, and you can miss the paragraph's whole job.
Ask what the paragraph does for the ones around it.
This one zooms all the way out. Not one sentence, but the shape of the whole passage.
Before the choices, sketch the shape. Claim, then example. Problem, then solution.
Then find the choice with the same moves in the same order. The right topic isn't enough.
Here's one. Read it with me.
First, a general pattern: most Arctic songbirds take the same routes. Then the tern breaks it. Pattern, then exception.
No hypothesis gets tested with experiments. And it's not told from one bird's point of view.
It does end on a debate, but about the tern's route. Not two theories of why birds migrate.
A general pattern, then one species as the exception.
A choice can name the right ideas and still get the order backwards.
Sketch the shape first, then match the moves in order.
Two authors disagree, and you're asked what they'd both still say. Sounds impossible. It isn't.
Split each passage in two: the facts it starts from, and the conclusion it reaches.
Authors who disagree usually share the facts. They're fighting about what those facts mean.
Here's one. Read it with me.
Passage one says social media boosts civic engagement. Passage two says it breeds isolation. B takes passage one's side.
Neither passage mentions regulation. And nobody calls in-person relationships entirely obsolete.
The fact under both arguments: social media has changed how people interact. Passage one needs that to be true too.
It's choice A. Same starting fact, opposite conclusions.
A tempting choice often restates one side. If only one author would sign it, it isn't common ground.
Separate facts from conclusions, then find the fact both authors stand on.
Here you predict a reply. One author hears the other's point. What do they say back?
Every author has one core value driving the argument. Name it in a few words.
Then let that value answer the new claim. Usually it accepts the facts and argues about what matters more.
Here's one. Read it with me.
Passage one cares about residents: better sleep, calmer neighborhoods. Its value is quality of life.
Calling the ordinance a mistake would flip passage one's whole position. B is out.
Denying that any business was hurt ignores the real losses passage two describes. And telling businesses to move cities goes way past anything passage one argues.
It's choice A. Sure, businesses feel it, but residents' quality of life matters more.
Skip replies that deny the other side's facts. A reasonable author admits them and argues about what they mean.
Find what the author cares about, then let that answer the new claim.
You get some notes and a goal. Here's the secret: almost every choice is true.
So don't ask which sentence is accurate. Ask which one does the exact job the goal names.
Goals are specific. One small phrase can rule out half the choices.
Here's one. Read it with me.
The goal: impact on staff work. Not patron convenience. That second part matters.
Shorter wait times help patrons, not staff. So A and C, built on wait times, miss the goal.
D calls the kiosks a technology investment. True enough, but it says nothing about staff.
Here's the staff note: more time helping patrons find books.
B pairs the kiosks with the staff note. Exactly what the goal asks.
Accurate isn't enough. The wrong choices here are true. They just serve a different goal.
Read the goal closely, then pick the sentence that does that exact job.
Transitions look like a vocab test. They're really a logic test.
Before you read a single choice, decide how the two sentences connect.
It's almost always one of four: contrast, cause and effect, addition, or example.
Only then find the word that signals that relationship. Don't test which one sounds right.
Here's one. Read it with me.
First sentence: the results looked promising.
Second sentence: the trials failed to replicate it. Good news, then bad news. That's a contrast.
The word similarly signals a match. The phrase for example signals an illustration. Neither is a contrast.
As a result would mean the good results caused the failure. They didn't.
The word however is the only contrast here. That's the answer.
Every choice can sound fine out loud. Only one matches the logic.
Name the relationship, then pick the word. Every time.
However and nonetheless both sound like contrast words. They're not quite the same.
The word however sets two opposite ideas side by side. This one, but that one.
The words nonetheless, still, and even so mean: yes, that happened, but this is true anyway.
So ask: do the ideas clash head on, or does the second hold up despite the first?
Here's one. Read it with me.
First sentence: the repairs ran months late. A setback.
Then the bridge passed every inspection. Being late doesn't cancel that. It's good news despite bad news.
The word consequently says the delay caused the clean inspection. It didn't.
And passing isn't similar to running late, or an example of it.
It's nonetheless. The setback is admitted, and the result still holds.
Contrast words aren't interchangeable. Concession means despite this, still. Not a flat contradiction.
Opposites side by side? However. True despite a setback? Nonetheless.
Two full sentences, one blank between them. There are only a few legal ways to glue them together.
First question, every time: could each side stand on its own as a full sentence? That's what an independent clause is.
If both sides are full sentences, use a period, a semicolon, or a comma plus a joining word like and or but.
A colon works only if the second part explains the first. A comma by itself never works. That's a comma splice.
Here's one. Read it with me.
Left side: the results were surprising. Subject, verb, complete thought. That's a sentence.
Right side: no one had predicted such a sharp decline. Also a full sentence. So a comma alone is a splice.
The word so, with no comma before it, runs them together. And the second part isn't a result of the first anyway.
Comma plus but is legal punctuation, but there's no contrast here. The second part explains why the results were surprising.
A semicolon joins two related full sentences, no joining word needed. That's the one.
A lone comma between two full sentences is the most popular wrong answer. It feels natural. It's still a splice.
Check both sides first. If they're both full sentences, you already know which choices can work.
Words like however look like they could glue sentences together. They can't. They need a strong mark on one side.
The word however isn't a joining word like but. Commas on both sides of it still leave you with a comma splice.
So one side needs something strong, a semicolon or a period, and the other side just gets a comma.
To pick the side, ask which sentence the however belongs to. What is it actually contrasting?
Here's one. Read it with me.
First sentence: engineers predicted the bridge would sag at forty tons. That's a full sentence.
Second: it held steady until fifty-five tons. Also full. However marks the contrast between the prediction and what happened.
So commas on both sides are a splice, and nothing before however runs the two sentences together.
A semicolon after however ties it to the prediction, where it contrasts with nothing.
Semicolon before however, comma after. However opens the second sentence, right where the contrast happens.
Comma, however, comma looks tidy. Between two full sentences, it's still a comma splice.
Figure out which sentence the transition belongs to. The strong mark goes at that sentence's edge, the comma inside it.
Some lists already have commas inside the items. Add more commas and nobody can tell who's who.
When every item is a single word or a short phrase, ordinary commas between them are fine.
But if even one item has its own comma, like a name and a job, switch to semicolons between the items.
And the list itself gets introduced by a colon, right after a full sentence.
Here's one. Read it with me.
Three volunteers organized the event. That's a full sentence announcing a list. A semicolon can't introduce a list. A colon can.
Choice C opens with a comma and drops the commas around each job. Two problems at once.
Now the colon choices. Each item is a name, a comma, then a job. With commas everywhere, you can't tell where one volunteer ends.
Colon to open, semicolons between people, commas inside each one. Three volunteers, easy to tell apart.
Don't overcorrect. Muffins, scones, and croissants don't need semicolons. No commas inside the items, no semicolons.
Look inside each item. If any one of them has a comma, the whole list switches to semicolons.
Some phrases are just bonus info. Drop them and the sentence still works. Those get boxed off with commas.
Ask one thing: do you need this phrase to know who or what the sentence means? If yes, no commas.
If it's just extra detail, box it off with commas, like parentheses you could lift right out.
In the middle of a sentence, that means a comma on both sides. At the very start or end, just one.
Here's one. Read it with me.
My uncle Raymond. The name already tells us exactly who this is.
So a retired firefighter is extra detail. Lift it out and the sentence still works. It needs commas.
It sits mid-sentence, so it needs a comma on each side. One choice opens without closing. The other closes without opening.
Commas on both sides. The extra detail is boxed in, and Raymond still volunteers.
The half-boxed version is the sneaky one. One comma looks almost right. In the middle, you need the pair.
If you can drop it, box it. Commas on both sides in the middle, one at the edges.
Not every sentence is two sentences glued together. Sometimes only one side can stand on its own.
These start with a lead-in phrase, like despite the storm, followed by a full sentence.
The lead-in can't stand on its own. So a period or a semicolon is wrong. Those need full sentences on both sides.
The fix is almost always a single comma, right where the lead-in ends and the main sentence starts.
Here's one. Read it with me.
The flight departed on time. That's a full sentence. Now the front part: despite the storm. Could that stand alone?
Nope. So a semicolon, which needs a full sentence on both sides, is out.
No comma at all runs the lead-in into the sentence. And a comma after despite splits it from the storm.
One comma, right after the word storm. Lead-in, comma, sentence.
Once you learn the semicolon rule, it's tempting everywhere. Check both sides first. Here only one side is a sentence.
A lead-in phrase before a full sentence gets one comma. Not a semicolon, not a period.
Plural, possessive, plural possessive. Out loud they sound exactly the same, so your ear is no help here.
First ask: does the noun own the word right after it? If nothing's owned, it's a plain plural. No apostrophe.
If it owns something, count the owners. One owner gets apostrophe s. A plural ending in s just gets an apostrophe after the s.
Here's one. Read it with me.
Right after the blank comes identities. Those belong to the ghostwriters. So we need a possessive, not a plain plural.
And the sentence says two. More than one owner. The apostrophe s version would mean just one ghostwriter.
The last one adds apostrophe s after the s. That's not a real form. A plural ending in s just takes the apostrophe.
Ghostwriters, with the apostrophe after the s. Two owners, one possessive.
Don't sprinkle apostrophes on every plural. If nothing after the word belongs to it, there's no apostrophe.
Is something owned? If not, plain plural. If so, count the owners, then place the apostrophe.
Here's the sneaky one. Sometimes the right answer adds no punctuation at all.
When three choices add a comma or a semicolon, it's easy to assume one must be needed. Not always.
Some words go together with nothing between them: a subject and its verb, a verb and its object, a preposition and its object.
Run the same check as always. What's on each side of the mark? If there's no real boundary, leave it clean.
Here's one. Read it with me.
The blank holds the words during the, right before performance. During is a preposition, and the performance is its object.
A comma or a semicolon after during splits it from its object. And a semicolon needs full sentences on both sides anyway.
A comma after the word the cuts it off from performance, breaking one little phrase in half.
During the performance, with no marks inside. It's one unit, so it stays together.
A comma in the choices isn't a hint. Don't add one just because it's on the menu.
Check what's on each side. If nothing needs separating, the cleanest choice wins.
A colon basically says, here's what I mean. And it's less picky than a semicolon about what comes after it.
The rule lives on the left. Everything before a colon has to stand on its own as a full sentence.
After it, you can have a list, a short phrase, or a sentence that explains the first one.
That's the difference from a semicolon, which needs full sentences on both sides.
Here's one. Read it with me.
Left side ends with: the team packed everything they would need. That's a full sentence, and it promises something.
Right side: tents, dried food, water filters, and a satellite phone. That's a list, not a sentence. So no semicolon.
A comma doesn't introduce a list after a full sentence. And like would make these just examples, when it's everything they needed.
The colon. A full sentence on the left, and here's what I mean on the right.
Don't treat a colon like a semicolon. Only the left side has to be a full sentence.
Check the left side. If it's a full sentence that sets something up, the colon delivers it.
Is this sentence asking a question, or just talking about one? That decides the word order and the ending.
If a question is tucked inside a statement, after words like wondered or asked, keep normal order and end with a period.
If the text asks the question itself, the helping verb comes before the subject, and it ends with a question mark.
Here's one. Read it with me.
Ines Varga wondered. The sentence is reporting what she wondered, not asking us anything. So it's an embedded question.
That means statement order: the snow lasted, not did the snow last. Both choices with did are out.
B has the right order but a question mark. The sentence is a statement, so it ends with a period.
Why the snow lasted so long, with a period. Statement order, statement ending.
There's a why in it, so a question mark feels right. But she wondered makes the whole thing a statement.
First decide whether the text asks or reports. The word order and the end mark follow from that.
A verb has to match its subject. The trick is that the subject gets buried under extra words.
Mentally cross out any phrase sitting between the subject and its verb.
Then match the verb to the real subject. One thing, singular verb. More than one, plural.
Here's one. Read it with me.
The phrase of the survey is just describing. Cross it out. Same with conducted across all twelve regions.
What's left: the results, blank, still being reviewed. Results means more than one. Plural.
Is, was, and has been are all singular. They'd match survey, but survey isn't the subject.
Are. Plural subject, plural verb.
A noun tucked inside an extra phrase is often a decoy. Match the verb to the real subject.
Cross out the extras, find the real subject, then match the verb.
Lists have a rhythm. Every item has to match the ones that came before it.
In a list, every item uses the same grammatical shape. That's called parallel structure.
Look at the first couple of items, notice their form, and make the last one match exactly.
Here's one. Read it with me.
Writing clear emails. Giving effective feedback. Both start with a word that ends the same way, in ing.
The choices to lead and leads switch shapes partway through the list. That breaks the rhythm.
Having led is closer, but it's still a different form. The list needs the same kind of word, like writing and giving.
Leading meetings efficiently. Writing, giving, leading. All three match.
Some choices are perfectly good English on their own. What matters is whether they match the rest of the list.
Spot the form of the first items, then make every item match it.
Pronoun questions are two checks in one: who it points to, and what job it's doing.
Find the noun the pronoun points back to. Is it one thing, or more than one?
Then check its job. Right before a noun, you need an owner word, like its or their, with no apostrophe.
Here's one. Read it with me.
Whose theory? Sorensen and Asante's. Two people, so it's plural.
Its, with no apostrophe, is singular. It would point to the ship, not two archaeologists.
